extracted.intended_audience: public relations students, practitioners, managers, and researchers evaluating PR programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and measurable criteria for designing, conducting, and using evaluation research to judge public relations programs (press relations, employee communication, community/educational relations), including methods, measures, and decision uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration: budget benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare administration of public relations by calculating average budgets and range of budgets so managers can compare their expenditures with similar units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AT&T calculated average budgets and budget ranges to allow unit managers to compare expenditures with similar units; useful as an administrative/program-level performance metric rather than a communication-effect measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press relations: measure whether communication occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether communication from organization to media/public has taken place (communication as behavior — movement of symbols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by counting press clippings and identifying whether items originated from company press representatives; note limitation: measuring contact does not prove messages were read by the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press relations: message content and theme alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze press coverage content to identify what messages were actually communicated and the extent to which media messages reflect the themes public relations intended to stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use content analysis (AT&T hired an outside firm) to tabulate themes and map media content to intended themes; track how many clippings carried intended messages and examples of message distortion or omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press relations: coverage valence (favorable/neutral/unfavorable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify and count press articles as favorable, neutral, or unfavorable to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate counts and use computer analyses to trace monthly/yearly trends; combine with origin and theme alignment measures to assess effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee communication: exposure (communication objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how many employees actually received company publications or communications (a measure of exposure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use yearly employee surveys or readership measures to count distribution/exposure; can be operationalized via receipt questions in questionnaires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee communication: message retention / accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how many employees remembered what certain articles said—used as a measure of 'accuracy' or message retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recall questions in employee surveys to assess retention; combine with comprehension/readability measures to interpret retention results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee communication: perceived understandability / readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess employees' perceptions of how understandable company publications are, and measure readability objectively as an evaluation of message quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readability indices and survey questions about perceived clarity; readability can be assessed separately and used to improve publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relations: activity frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Record how often community relations techniques (open houses, interviews with community leaders, talks to groups) are used in each community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frequency as a process metric to know whether planned outreach occurred and which techniques were used where.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relations: effects on retention, cognition acceptance, and overt behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure effects of community relations activities on message retention, acceptance of cognitions (beliefs), and overt behaviors of community leaders and residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up studies, interviews, and surveys of community leaders can link activities to cognitive and behavioral outcomes; use these as outcome evaluation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational relations: learning outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the extent to which schoolchildren learned themes relevant to the company from materials provided to schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tests, recall questions, or classroom assessments to determine whether educational materials transmitted intended themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 1 — Specify objectives from taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose specific, measurable objectives (communication, message retention, acceptance of cognitions, etc.) from the taxonomy developed earlier (Chapter 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should be realistic, measurable, and have known probabilities of success; selection drives what you will measure in later stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 2 — Measure the objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: For each specified objective, measure or observe whether it has been accomplished using appropriate instruments or observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measures mapped to each objective (e.g., exposure questions for communication objectives, recall for retention). The chapter promises sample measures for each objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 3 — Collect and analyze data
rubrics_metrics.description: Administer measures to a sample of the target public, compare results with expected effects, determine if objectives have been met, and diagnose reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze differences between observed outcomes and expectations; interpret why objectives were or were not met to make recommendations for program improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 4 — Report results to decision makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clear reports tailored to audiences: emphasize PR objective attainment to PR executives and explain contributions to organizational goals for top management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use understandable language and frame findings in terms of how PR accomplishment supports organizational goals and justifies programs/resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage 5 — Apply results to decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use evaluation results to change and improve programs; evaluations must inform decisions rather than be ignored when inconvenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using evaluation only to support existing programs; apply findings to continue/discontinue, improve, add/drop strategies, allocate resources, or adopt/reject program theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative vs evaluative research distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative research helps define the PR problem and communication objective; evaluative research determines whether the objective has been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formative techniques (Chapter 7 measures, planning in Chapter 8) before program launch; conduct evaluative research after implementation to judge outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic question — When to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask evaluative questions during planning (not only after program completion) so you correctly identify publics and problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine evaluation with studies to define publics; early evaluation questions prevent designing programs for the wrong problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic question — Where to evaluate (perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate not only from the organization's point of view but also from the audience's perspective; PR should affect both organization and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measures that capture effects on target publics, not just organizational activities or outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic question — How to evaluate (frequency/form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer continuous, repeated, smaller evaluations over large, one-shot studies to monitor program performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement process evaluations (monthly/yearly performance measures) to detect trends and guide ongoing adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic question — What to measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure concepts beyond demographics and attitudes (e.g., cognitive objectives used to define publics); demographics alone do not define publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measures such as exposure, retention, comprehension, acceptance of cognitions, and behaviors that map to chosen objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process evaluations (administration/performance measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a program is being administered effectively (process), not just whether outcomes occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ongoing performance indicators (e.g., monthly counts of favorable stories, employee exposure/comprehension/readability trends) to monitor program operation and staff performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should evaluate: insider vs outsider
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether evaluation will be conducted internally or by external consultants, weighing objectivity against insider knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outsiders are generally more objective but know less about programs and may find more problems; internal evaluators enable continuous process evaluation. Recommended: build internal research capability and hire consultants when needed for objectivity or specialized expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of methods: quantitative vs qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Select between quantitative methods (more objective, easier analysis) and qualitative methods (more detail and context) depending on evaluation goals and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative methods are suited for measurement and trend analysis; qualitative methods work well for formative research and understanding context. Consider costs, time, and the need for statistical analysis vs detailed insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys: general uses and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys are the most used PR research method for measuring objectives but cannot always prove causation or control exposure; they are useful for tracing effects when additional conditions are measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administer questionnaires to samples and measure relevant contextual variables to strengthen inferences about program effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey mode — personal interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal interviews: highest response rates and accuracy, can establish rapport and observe respondent care, but are costly and fewer interviews per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for community leaders or 'name' people who would be offended by telephone interviews; sampling and access can be difficult in urban areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey mode — telephone interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Telephone interviews: widely used, less expensive than personal interviews, facilitate national random samples (random digit dialing), and can be reasonably long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapport is harder and interviewers have less ability to judge answer quality, but telephone surveys are fast and suited for most PR studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey mode — mail questionnaires
rubrics_metrics.description: Mail questionnaires: can reach large samples, allow longer instruments and more thorough answers, but suffer from low response rates unless topic is salient or follow-ups are extensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for high-involvement publics (employees, association members) or panel studies where participants are paid and surveyed repeatedly; budget for follow-ups to raise response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments: establishing causality and design options
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled experiments can establish time order and stronger causal inferences; four practical designs: pretest-posttest, posttest-only with randomization, multiple pretest-posttest, and nonequivalent control group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field experiments are common but perfect control is often impossible; be prepared to use quasi-experimental or nonexperimental designs when random assignment or comparable control groups are not feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary data use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commercial, academic, or organizational secondary data when original research is unaffordable; such data can suggest program effects but rarely prove that a program worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reanalyze available datasets or piggyback onto internal surveys (personnel, marketing) but ensure the sample/population aligns with your target public and timing relative to the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative research characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative research is naturalistic, contextualized, uses maximized comparisons, and employs sensitized concepts to capture participants' own language and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics support rich contextual insights; qualitative work should be theory-guided (sensitizing concepts) but open to unexpected findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative methods — observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative observation can be participant observation or onlooker observation, and covert or overt; researchers use theory as guidance but do not limit observations strictly to predefined concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participant observers experience the program; onlookers simply watch. Be mindful of ethical issues, observer effects, and training required for objective observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative methods — interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Three interview approaches: informal conversational, general interview guide, and standardized open-end interview; choose based on desired structure and flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal interviews are exploratory; guided interviews seek certain effects but allow flexibility; standardized open-end asks the same questions but allows probing for unanticipated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative methods — focus groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus groups invite a small, typical group of the target public to discuss prepared questions in a neutral setting; members respond and react to each other's ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus groups reveal group dynamics and natural conversational evaluations but risk group influence/bandwagon effects; useful as formative technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mixed methods appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Both quantitative and qualitative methods have roles: qualitative methods work best in formative evaluations; combining methods yields richer, actionable insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resources are limited, skilled qualitative work can substitute for quantitative data, but managers often prefer numeric evidence. Aim to triangulate findings across methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time budgets (activity/time allocation measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track how people spend time (diary, recall interview, or random-interval observation) to measure media consumption, employee exposure to company media, or PR staff time allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three calculation methods: hourly diaries (most detailed but reactive), next-day recall interviews, and random-time spot checks (reduce reactivity and provide representative snapshots). Useful for internal management control and billing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question design — open vs closed-end questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose closed-end questions when possible because they are easier for respondents and simpler to analyze; use open-end for qualitative or exploratory probes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed-end formats support quantitative scaling; open-end questions are valuable for probes and exploratory insights in formative research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (demographic) questions best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask demographic/fact questions (sex, age, income, media usage) as closed multiple-choice items; generally provide about five response choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: age groups with five categories; choose response categories appropriate to analysis plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative question types (beliefs and attitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure beliefs and attitudes using multiple-choice ratings, Likert-type agreement scales (use five points including neutral), semantic differential scales (polar adjectives on a 7-point scale), or rankings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use several measures of the same attitude and sum into a single scale when appropriate; provide neutral midpoints for Likert items and use consistent scaling for semantic differential items.
